highlights.titleZh: Journal of Medical Internet Research - Medical Reasoning in Large Language Models: Development and Evaluation of the MedEvalArena Benchmark
highlights.content: ### Abstract Background: Large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on medical specialty board multiple-choice questions (MCQs) but underperform in complex medical reasoning. This gap indicates a need to improve LLM medical reasoning and evaluation paradigms. Objective: This study aimed to develop and evaluate MedEvalArena, a dynamically regenerable benchmark for assessing medical reasoning in LLMs. Methods: In a symmetric round-robin format, 6 frontier LLMs from the OpenAI, Grok, Gemini, Claude, Kimi, and DeepSeek families generated challenging board-style medical MCQs, adjudicated question validity on an ensemble LLM-as-judge panel, and answered the validated examination. Candidate items were generated until each model contributed 50 validated questions according to Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC)/American Board of Medical Specialties (ABMS) physician specialty distributions, yielding a 300-question examination. Judges adjudicated candidate questions’ logical validity and medical accuracy. We compared question-generation validity rates, assessed leave-one-out judge agreement, and tested for self-judging preference. Questions were audited for overlap with public MedQA (medical question-answering) benchmarks. We tested question-answering (QA) accuracy across LLMs using a binomial-logit generalized linear mixed model likelihood-ratio test. A generator-stratified 90-question subset was completed by 5 board-certified physicians for paired human-LLM analysis. We evaluated inference cost-accuracy tradeoffs. Multiple comparisons were adjusted by the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure. Results: Judge-panel validity rates were significantly higher for questions generated by OpenAI (94.8%, Wilson 95% CI 85.9%-98.2%), Gemini (92.3%, 95% CI 83.2%-96.7%), and Claude (83.3%, 95% CI 72.6%-90.4%) models than those generated by Kimi (63.8%, 95% CI 54.3%-72.4%), Grok (56%, 95% CI 45.8%-65.8%), and DeepSeek (46.0%, 95% CI 37.4%-54.7%). Kimi also demonstrated significantly higher validity than DeepSeek (2-sample tests of proportions; BH-adjusted *P*=.01). The public-source similarity audit found no exact or near-duplicate matches. Leave-one-out judge agreement was moderate. Generator-specific same-family judging coefficients were nonnegative (0 to 11.0 percentage points); however, none remained significant after BH adjustment. There was no significant difference between the 6 frontier LLM QA accuracies, which ranged from 85.7% (257/300) to 91.7% (275/300), on the 300-question examination (generalized linear mixed model likelihood-ratio test *P*=.07). The study had 80% power to detect LLM accuracy differences of 9.2 percentage points; nonsignificance did not establish equivalence. On the 90-question subset, physician accuracy was 85.6% (95% CI 79.4%‐91.7%; stratified normal with finite-population correction), compared with aggregate LLM performance of 94.4% (85/90; Wilson 95% CI 87.6%‐97.6%). This difference was not significant (McNemar test, *P*=.08); however, the study was powered to detect a human vs LLM accuracy difference of 14% to 15%. Answering-only costs varied by nearly 2 orders of magnitude, with multiple models on the cost-accuracy Pareto frontier. Conclusions: MedEvalArena enables scalable, regenerable, peer-judged benchmarking of LLM medical reasoning. highlights.content: # GPT-6.2 Astra scores 41.2% on Ember-0 robotics benchmark, more than doubling its predecessor Photo: Steve A Johnson / Pexels OpenAI's latest Astra model posts big gains in robot control, including the first reported success on deformable-object tasks OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Astra has scored 41.2% on Ember-0, a robotics benchmark maintained by XDOF. Two months ago, its predecessor managed 19.6%. ## What the numbers show XDOF reported the Ember-0 result on November 20, 2026. The previous model, GPT-6 Astra, posted its 19.6% in September 2026. On a separate benchmark, AA-Robotics v0.1, GPT-6.2 Astra scored 79 out of 100. It also used fewer arm commands than the other models tested. Speed improved too. Average prediction latency across the Astra series fell from 15.0 seconds to 10.1 seconds between model versions. ## The t-shirt problem The most striking claim attached to GPT-6.2 Astra is qualitative rather than numerical. It is described as the first model to demonstrate success on deformable-object tasks. Those include handling a t-shirt and tying a knot. To a human, these are chores. To a robot, they are notoriously hard. ### AI, tech, and the markets they move—in one daily briefing. Daily. Free. Join 34,000+ readers across crypto, finance, and policy. A rigid object like a block or a cup keeps its shape, so a model can predict where every part of it will be after a move. Fabric and rope do not cooperate. Every tug changes the shape of the whole object, which means the model has to keep re-reading the scene and adjusting on the fly. ## Background: language models as robot brains The Astra results land as frontier AI labs increasingly test large language models as controllers for robots. The idea is that a model trained on vast amounts of text and imagery can translate instructions into physical actions. The GPT-6.x line has been part of that push. The progression from GPT-6 Astra to GPT-6.2 Astra reflects ongoing refinement within the series. Benchmarks like Ember-0 and AA-Robotics v0.1 exist to keep that confidence honest. They put models through standardized tasks so that progress can be measured instead of merely claimed. ## What this means The headline number deserves both credit and context. A 41.2% score is a large improvement, but it also means the model still falls short on the majority of what Ember-0 measures. Latency is still the obvious weak point. An average of 10.1 seconds per prediction is far better than 15.0 seconds, but it remains slow for anything that needs to react in real time. A model that leads on Ember-0 while also posting a 79 out of 100 on AA-Robotics v0.1 puts pressure on rivals to show comparable physical-world performance, not just strong chatbot scores. **Disclosure:** This article was edited by Diego Almada Lopez. highlights.content: **Agentic AI Risk Management is Not Sufficiently Developed** The progress of AI has been dizzying, and agentic AI is at the leading edge. At the end of 2025, AI agents helped streamline simple coding tasks; by the end of this year, they were building complex software autonomously. Mathematics agents went from solving hard mathematics problems in 2025 to exceeding the abilities of the best human mathematicians in 2026. Naturally, great optimism has developed that AI agents can make these prodigious gains in other areas, resulting in a gold rush of AI agent development: Eric Schmidt, the former CEO of Google, advised in early 2026 that “if you really want to make money, it’s actually easy. Found an agentic AI company…I mean, build an agent to do something. This is the agentic period in AI.”\[1] One rush of AI companies has been towards AI agents that can access financial accounts and help their users pay bills, manage investments and make financial decisions. This prospect, while promising, exposes a lag between AI agents’ rapid development and nascent risk management practices, especially for financial applications. Right now, the risk that an AI agent could make mistaken or fraudulent financial decisions is high. Because banks and other financial institutions are responsible for the safety of the funds and assets their customers have entrusted to them and are the only place to call when anything goes wrong, they have attempted to restrict unvetted AI agents from accessing bank accounts.\[2] It remains to be seen whether such efforts will continue to be necessary and practical. In this post, using Meta Muse as an example, we give a primer on how AI agents work, review the nascent field of AI agentic risk management and describe how AI agentic risk management has been currently implemented. We show that current AI agentic risk management practices are not sufficient for bank and financial institution security needs. Until agentic AI risk management practices are robust enough to make accessing financial accounts safe, banks and other financial institutions should attempt to block agent access over unapproved channels and warn customers that they allow agent access to bank accounts at their own risk. The three safety issues surrounding AI agents more generally could impose significant harm on consumers if agents are allowed to access bank accounts before risk management practices catch up with rapid technological development. These three issues are: 1. An agent made a mistake. 2. An agent solved the wrong problem. 3. An agent became the victim of fraud. Agentic risk management is not currently sufficiently well-developed for banks to effectively manage these risks, therefore making it unsafe for agents to access bank accounts. First, it’s useful to understand how AI agents work. ### What is an AI agent? Most people are familiar with AI from using chatbots such as ChatGPT or Claude. In these AI applications, the user interacts with a Large Language Model (LLM) by asking questions and making comments. The model replies. Current LLMs are also capable of sophisticated reasoning. For example, they can solve complex mathematics problems. Many LLMs are multi-modal as well: they can receive text, pictures or sound as input and respond with text, pictures or sound. But by themselves, LLMs cannot do anything other than communicate with the user. If we want an LLM to do work, we must put significant coding around it, called the harness. The harness is what turns the LLM into an AI agent. The LLM is like the brain and the harness is like the body. The LLM works with the harness to do work. highlights.content: # AutoRAGBench: A Benchmark for LLM Agents Automating RAG System DevelopmentThanks: \*The authors contribute equally to this work.Thanks: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible. ###### Abstract Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a well-established paradigm for augmenting large language models (LLMs) with information retrieved from external corpora. However, developing effective RAG systems requires substantial engineering effort and iterative experimentation, as effective design choices vary across tasks and domains. With rapid advances in LLM agent capabilities, we ask how well these agents can autonomously build RAG systems and how effectively they can improve them through iteration. In this paper, we propose AutoRAGBench, the first benchmark to evaluate how well LLM agents develop RAG systems from scratch in an open code space. It comprises nine RAG system development tasks. For each task, agents build RAG systems from scratch without starter code or prescribed strategies, under a six-hour budget on a single H800 GPU. They analyze task data, implement RAG pipelines, and iteratively refine their designs based on experimental feedback. We evaluate nine agent configurations and analyze both the effectiveness of the resulting RAG systems and their development trajectories. GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI achieves the highest average score of 56.1. The composite Human-SOTA baseline averages 44.4. These results show that LLM agents can automate effective RAG system development. When starting from a human-designed system on each of seven tasks, GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI improves the score by 16.6 points on average while preserving the methods’ core mechanisms. ###### Index Terms: LLM, Agent, RAG, Benchmark ## I Introduction Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) \[1, 2, 3] is a well-established paradigm that augments large language models (LLMs) with information retrieved from external corpora. Retrieved evidence grounds answers in traceable sources, and RAG also supports updates to the external corpus \[4]. However, accurate and efficient RAG requires task-specific design choices, such as how to process the corpus, build the index, retrieve information, and select evidence \[5]. Multi-hop questions\[6, 7] require combining evidence across documents, whereas knowledge-graph questions \[8] require entity linking and graph traversal. Developers must therefore choose RAG methods suited to the corpus and the questions users ask, then iteratively improve the system based on test results. As shown in Fig. 1, a business owner wants an intelligent question-answering (QA) assistant for employees who need information from internal documents. A RAG system can power this assistant by retrieving passages relevant to each question and supplying them to the LLM as evidence for its answer \[9]. Manually building an effective RAG system is difficult and time-consuming because developers must analyze the documents, select and implement a retrieval strategy, evaluate its performance on example questions, and refine it based on the results. Recent advances in LLM agents \[10, 11] have enabled them to automate much of this development cycle. These capabilities motivate our research question. How well can LLM agents autonomously build RAG systems across tasks, and how effectively can they improve these systems through iteration? Existing studies do not directly address this question. First, prior work on RAG evaluation \[12, 13, 14, 15] examines how individual components and workflow configurations affect system performance and whether the resulting answers are accurate and supported by the retrieved evidence. These evaluations do not support analysis of LLM agents’ ability to develop RAG systems. highlights.title: Q&A: Enabling more human-like interactions and understanding in multimodal foundation models | MIT News | Massachusetts Institute of Technology

highlights.content: ### Press Contact: *Humans experience and interact with the world through sensory information. This could mean learning correspondences between the sound of bird chirps and the word “robin,” or being able to visually identify and follow your friend “Sarah” in a crowd of people. In many cases, people are able to draw on their latent “multimodal” knowledge — information across multiple data types, from audio to video to text or spoken word — to perform these tasks without many, or sometimes even any, examples.* *Multimodal foundation models of artificial intelligence are increasingly gaining capabilities that mimic this. However, their apparent multimodal fluency often belies their actual understanding. An MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab team, co-led by Jim Glass, senior research scientist in the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, has been investigating critical failures of state-of-the-art multimodal models and developing benchmarks and data-efficient methods to overcome these performance gaps with limited supervision. He speaks about this work in the following interview.* **Q:** What were your goals for this project, and why would you opt to address AI models’ weaknesses over scaling to larger models? **A:** This project has been going on for many years now, with roughly the same MIT-IBM team of speech and vision experts. We've wanted to explore the relationship between perception (things that you see and hear) and language, largely speaking: We have all of this absorbed knowledge and language skills, text-based, in the form of a large language model, so we wanted to know how you can relate them without using a whole bunch of annotated training data. Sometimes the models have seen certain phenomena, a latent representation of something that they have internally, but maybe due to subsequent fine-tuning or something, it disappears, so, developing techniques to try to make this capability re-emerge is a useful thing. As you study these publicly available models, you can see weaknesses even in big ones, so I think it's important to try to address these limitations. If you had an unlimited budget, you could go out and create the annotations that you need, but it's also good to be able to try to get these models to learn more on their own. We’ve done that by creating novel benchmarks that we can evaluate against, then developing techniques that perform better on these benchmarks, and getting these models to learn on their own. Throughout our research collaboration — and this has very much been a strong collaboration between MIT and IBM — we have continued to release public benchmarks for people to use, and that's a lasting artifact. I think the overriding themes are multimodalities with language models, trying to address the shortcomings of these models, and trying to develop techniques that do not require a lot of annotated data to complete tasks better. **Q:** Can you walk us through how the project has evolved? **A:** When we first started this project, we were trying to build models that could learn correspondences automatically, not telling the machine anything more than, “This audio caption goes with this picture,” sort of like reading a picture book to a child who's learning language. We would just show it these matching examples, and we'd show it mismatching examples. They could learn that the sequence of sounds that says “lighthouse” corresponds to a picture of a lighthouse, without any text being involved. Moving beyond speech was to include general audio, and then we started looking at video instead of still images. We would train the model, showing it matching video sequences with the corresponding audio stream and then mismatching ones, and make it reconstruct them. We would also mask some of the images or the audio, and have the model reconstruct it. The model would learn strong relationships; then, far beyond speech, it would learn what parrots sound like, or electric guitars versus acoustic g...

highlights.content: # Apple seems to be building its own AI agent. This could be bad news for Meta’s Muse. AI Agents.content: **Agentic AI Risk Management is Not Sufficiently Developed** The progress of AI has been dizzying, and agentic AI is at the leading edge. At the end of 2025, AI agents helped streamline simple coding tasks; by the end of this year, they were building complex software autonomously. Mathematics agents went from solving hard mathematics problems in 2025 to exceeding the abilities of the best human mathematicians in 2026. Naturally, great optimism has developed that AI agents can make these prodigious gains in other areas, resulting in a gold rush of AI agent development: Eric Schmidt, the former CEO of Google, advised in early 2026 that “if you really want to make money, it’s actually easy. Found an agentic AI company…I mean, build an agent to do something. This is the agentic period in AI.”\[1] One rush of AI companies has been towards AI agents that can access financial accounts and help their users pay bills, manage investments and make financial decisions. This prospect, while promising, exposes a lag between AI agents’ rapid development and nascent risk management practices, especially for financial applications. Right now, the risk that an AI agent could make mistaken or fraudulent financial decisions is high. Because banks and other financial institutions are responsible for the safety of the funds and assets their customers have entrusted to them and are the only place to call when anything goes wrong, they have attempted to restrict unvetted AI agents from accessing bank accounts.\[2] It remains to be seen whether such efforts will continue to be necessary and practical. In this post, using Meta Muse as an example, we give a primer on how AI agents work, review the nascent field of AI agentic risk management and describe how AI agentic risk management has been currently implemented. We show that current AI agentic risk management practices are not sufficient for bank and financial institution security needs. Until agentic AI risk management practices are robust enough to make accessing financial accounts safe, banks and other financial institutions should attempt to block agent access over unapproved channels and warn customers that they allow agent access to bank accounts at their own risk. The three safety issues surrounding AI agents more generally could impose significant harm on consumers if agents are allowed to access bank accounts before risk management practices catch up with rapid technological development. These three issues are: 1. An agent made a mistake. 2. An agent solved the wrong problem. 3. An agent became the victim of fraud. For example, they can solve complex mathematics problems. Many LLMs are multi-modal as well: they can receive text, pictures or sound as input and respond with text, pictures or sound. But by themselves, LLMs cannot do anything other than communicate with the user. If we want an LLM to do work, we must put significant coding around it, called the harness. The harness is what turns the LLM into an AI agent. The LLM is like the brain and the harness is like the body. The LLM works with the harness to do work. AI Agents.content: # The Next Big Tech Monopoly Could Be Your Personal AI Agent George Colville / Nov 20, 2026 Muse, Dots, Duet, Spark, Copilot, Grok Bot. Agentic AI is now a mass-market consumer product. In tech hubs like San Francisco, New York, and London, expert users have been employing agents, both individually and in swarms, on work tasks and side projects. They have used agents to build personal apps, run cafes, book restaurants and tennis courts, evaluate health insurance plans, and register with new doctors. Until now, this was the prerogative of the tech-savvy. That is about to change. This is no bad thing. The prospect of democratizing the time- and labor-saving benefits of agentic AI beyond expert users is exciting. That promise, however, comes with potential peril. Beyond the cybersecurity and privacy risks, and the societal upheaval as systems built for a time before AI strain under its pressure, lies a deeper, systemic threat. This is the possibility that an agentic AI monopoly or oligopoly concentrates extraordinary power in the hands of a small number of private corporations. In a new report, “New Gateway, Same Gatekeepers,” we examine this threat, identify the economic and democratic risks it poses to society, and set out what we can do to avert it. ## Personal agents: the endgame for consumer AI While the high priests of AI continue to prophesy artificial general intelligence, the industry built around them has been hard at work designing products it can sell. Unlike businesses, which have been experimenting with agentic AI for months or even years, consumer interactions with AI have generally been limited to conversations with chatbots. That changed a few months ago. Since mid-2026, all the major AI players – OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google, Microsoft, and xAI – have released new accessible personal AI agents that can act on people’s behalf. The ambition for these companies is simple: to create and monetize a personal assistant that can automate as many daily tasks as possible. They want, in other words, to become a universal digital intermediary: a single platform through which people buy their groceries and their clothes, book their holidays, interact with government services, control their homes, consume news, and communicate with their friends, family, and communities. Instead of dozens of apps and websites, the intention is for one single personal assistant with a text or voice interface to be the only interface people interact with for most of their digital needs. This vision is compelling. It could free people up to spend more time with their friends and families, on their hobbies, and on their work. At the same time, it raises deeply troubling questions for individual autonomy, economic fairness, and democracy. ## New digital gatekeepers with unprecedented power While the promise of personal agents is vast, there is a real risk that one or a small number of companies come to dominate the technology, establishing an agentic AI monopoly or oligopoly. In doing so, these corporations would become the arbiters of what people buy and who they buy it from, would select which news they receive, and would shape how they communicate with their friends, family, and communities. They could do this fairly, but commercial pressure and the lack of competitive incentives to treat customers well will almost certainly push them in more harmful directions. With access to vast quantities of personal data, and acting on users’ behalf as a kind of digital exoskeleton, they would open the door to new extremes of surveillance and exploitation, both political and commercial. A concentrated market would create gatekeeper dynamics even more extreme than Amazon’s, Google’s and Apple’s existing versions. An agentic AI gatekeeper could charge excessive commissions to merchants that sell their products to people via AI agents. It might prioritize answers and actions that favor partners and advertisers, turning the entire economy into a pay-to-play...

LLMs.titleZh: Journal of Medical Internet Research - Medical Reasoning in Large Language Models: Development and Evaluation of the MedEvalArena Benchmark
LLMs.content: ### Abstract Background: Large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on medical specialty board multiple-choice questions (MCQs) but underperform in complex medical reasoning. This gap indicates a need to improve LLM medical reasoning and evaluation paradigms. Objective: This study aimed to develop and evaluate MedEvalArena, a dynamically regenerable benchmark for assessing medical reasoning in LLMs. Methods: In a symmetric round-robin format, 6 frontier LLMs from the OpenAI, Grok, Gemini, Claude, Kimi, and DeepSeek families generated challenging board-style medical MCQs, adjudicated question validity on an ensemble LLM-as-judge panel, and answered the validated examination. Candidate items were generated until each model contributed 50 validated questions according to Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC)/American Board of Medical Specialties (ABMS) physician specialty distributions, yielding a 300-question examination. Judges adjudicated candidate questions’ logical validity and medical accuracy. LLMs.titleZh: GPT-6.2 Astra scores 41.2% on Ember-0 robotics benchmark, more than doubling its predecessor
LLMs.content: # GPT-6.2 Astra scores 41.2% on Ember-0 robotics benchmark, more than doubling its predecessor Photo: Steve A Johnson / Pexels OpenAI's latest Astra model posts big gains in robot control, including the first reported success on deformable-object tasks OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Astra has scored 41.2% on Ember-0, a robotics benchmark maintained by XDOF. Two months ago, its predecessor managed 19.6%. ## What the numbers show XDOF reported the Ember-0 result on November 20, 2026. The previous model, GPT-6 Astra, posted its 19.6% in September 2026. On a separate benchmark, AA-Robotics v0.1, GPT-6.2 Astra scored 79 out of 100. It also used fewer arm commands than the other models tested. Speed improved too. Average prediction latency across the Astra series fell from 15.0 seconds to 10.1 seconds between model versions. ## The t-shirt problem The most striking claim attached to GPT-6.2 Astra is qualitative rather than numerical. It is described as the first model to demonstrate success on deformable-object tasks. Those include handling a t-shirt and tying a knot. To a human, these are chores. To a robot, they are notoriously hard. ### AI, tech, and the markets they move—in one daily briefing. Daily. Free. Join 34,000+ readers across crypto, finance, and policy. A rigid object like a block or a cup keeps its shape, so a model can predict where every part of it will be after a move. Fabric and rope do not cooperate. Every tug changes the shape of the whole object, which means the model has to keep re-reading the scene and adjusting on the fly. ## Background: language models as robot brains The Astra results land as frontier AI labs increasingly test large language models as controllers for robots. The idea is that a model trained on vast amounts of text and imagery can translate instructions into physical actions. The GPT-6.x line has been part of that push. The progression from GPT-6 Astra to GPT-6.2 Astra reflects ongoing refinement within the series. Benchmarks like Ember-0 and AA-Robotics v0.1 exist to keep that confidence honest. They put models through standardized tasks so that progress can be measured instead of merely claimed. ## What this means The headline number deserves both credit and context. A 41.2% score is a large improvement, but it also means the model still falls short on the majority of what Ember-0 measures. Latency is still the obvious weak point. An average of 10.1 seconds per prediction is far better than 15.0 seconds, but it remains slow for anything that needs to react in real time. A model that leads on Ember-0 while also posting a 79 out of 100 on AA-Robotics v0.1 puts pressure on rivals to show comparable physical-world performance, not just strong chatbot scores. **Disclosure:** This article was edited by Diego Almada Lopez. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible. ###### Abstract Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a well-established paradigm for augmenting large language models (LLMs) with information retrieved from external corpora. However, developing effective RAG systems requires substantial engineering effort and iterative experimentation, as effective design choices vary across tasks and domains. With rapid advances in LLM agent capabilities, we ask how well these agents can autonomously build RAG systems and how effectively they can improve them through iteration. In this paper, we propose AutoRAGBench, the first benchmark to evaluate how well LLM agents develop RAG systems from scratch in an open code space. It comprises nine RAG system development tasks. For each task, agents build RAG systems from scratch without starter code or prescribed strategies, under a six-hour budget on a single H800 GPU. They analyze task data, implement RAG pipelines, and iteratively refine their designs based on experimental feedback. We evaluate nine agent configurations and analyze both the effectiveness of the resulting RAG systems and their development trajectories. GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI achieves the highest average score of 56.1. The composite Human-SOTA baseline averages 44.4. These results show that LLM agents can automate effective RAG system development. When starting from a human-designed system on each of seven tasks, GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI improves the score by 16.6 points on average while preserving the methods’ core mechanisms. ###### Index Terms: LLM, Agent, RAG, Benchmark ## I Introduction Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) \[1, 2, 3] is a well-established paradigm that augments large language models (LLMs) with information retrieved from external corpora. Retrieved evidence grounds answers in traceable sources, and RAG also supports updates to the external corpus \[4]. However, accurate and efficient RAG requires task-specific design choices, such as how to process the corpus, build the index, retrieve information, and select evidence \[5]. Multi-hop questions\[6, 7] require combining evidence across documents, whereas knowledge-graph questions \[8] require entity linking and graph traversal. Developers must therefore choose RAG methods suited to the corpus and the questions users ask, then iteratively improve the system based on test results. LLMs.content: ### Press Contact: *Humans experience and interact with the world through sensory information. This could mean learning correspondences between the sound of bird chirps and the word “robin,” or being able to visually identify and follow your friend “Sarah” in a crowd of people. In many cases, people are able to draw on their latent “multimodal” knowledge — information across multiple data types, from audio to video to text or spoken word — to perform these tasks without many, or sometimes even any, examples.* *Multimodal foundation models of artificial intelligence are increasingly gaining capabilities that mimic this. However, their apparent multimodal fluency often belies their actual understanding. An MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab team, co-led by Jim Glass, senior research scientist in the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, has been investigating critical failures of state-of-the-art multimodal models and developing benchmarks and data-efficient methods to overcome these performance gaps with limited supervision. He speaks about this work in the following interview.* **Q:** What were your goals for this project, and why would you opt to address AI models’ weaknesses over scaling to larger models? **A:** This project has been going on for many years now, with roughly the same MIT-IBM team of speech and vision experts. We've wanted to explore the relationship between perception (things that you see and hear) and language, largely speaking: We have all of this absorbed knowledge and language skills, text-based, in the form of a large language model, so we wanted to know how you can relate them without using a whole bunch of annotated training data. Sometimes the models have seen certain phenomena, a latent representation of something that they have internally, but maybe due to subsequent fine-tuning or something, it disappears, so, developing techniques to try to make this capability re-emerge is a useful thing. As you study these publicly available models, you can see weaknesses even in big ones, so I think it's important to try to address these limitations. If you had an unlimited budget, you could go out and create the annotations that you need, but it's also good to be able to try to get these models to learn more on their own. We’ve done that by creating novel benchmarks that we can evaluate against, then developing techniques that perform better on these benchmarks, and getting these models to learn on their own. Throughout our research collaboration — and this has very much been a strong collaboration between MIT and IBM — we have continued to release public benchmarks for people to use, and that's a lasting artifact. We would train the model, showing it matching video sequences with the corresponding audio stream and then mismatching ones, and make it reconstruct them. We would also mask some of the images or the audio, and have the model reconstruct it. LLMs.content: ## Abstract Large language models may facilitate unlawful activities, yet this risk remains underexplored in studies assessing illicit-content recognition or narrow categories of illicit scenarios. We define complicit facilitation as model guidance that assists users with illicit instructions. To assess it, we develop a legally-informed, automated pipeline grounded in real-world cases and legal frameworks, and introduce EVIL, a benchmark covering 269 illicit scenarios and 50 illicit intents across Chinese and United States legal contexts. Evaluations indicate that complicit facilitation is widespread across models, with legal warnings and lawful alternatives often omitted. Risks vary across socio-legal contexts and are elevated for crimes against societal interests, non-violent offenses, and intents involving subjective motives or deceptive justifications. Models provide more complicit assistance when instructions describe users as older adults, racial minorities, non-religious individuals, or workers in lower-prestige occupations. Existing open-source safety benchmarks and alignment datasets offer limited coverage and mitigation of these risks. ## Introduction Large language models (LLMs) have become ubiquitous information assistants in everyday practice, with billions of users relying on these models across diverse tasks1,2, such as writing assistance3,4,5, educational support6,7, and legal analysis8,9. The widespread adoption of these models has introduced critical safety risks, notably the concerning tendency for LLMs to provide assistance even when users submit prompts asking for help with illicit activities10,11, such as cybercrime and actions involving chemical or biological hazards12,13,14,15,16. Such activities pose significant threats to public safety and societal welfare, and these threats are magnified by the rapid growth in LLM deployment, making such illicit assistance a matter of urgent public concern. Existing research that evaluates LLMs regarding illegal activities either focuses solely on assessing whether models can recognize illicit risks—for example, by posing questions such as “Which of the following behaviors is considered an illegal cyber attack?”10, failing to evaluate the risk of LLMs providing assistance to illicit requests; or confines their scope to a narrow subset of illicit contexts11,13, such as instructions for manufacturing dangerous chemical or biological agents, capturing only limited illegal scenarios and illicit intents. In fact, real-world illegal activities encompass a broad spectrum of scenarios, spanning hundreds of distinct types of offenses17. Moreover, the motivations underlying illicit requests exhibit considerable complexity, shaped by diverse factors such as the specific objectives of users (e.g., seeking tools to commit a crime, identifying optimal timing or location) and the temporal context of the requests (e.g., premeditated planning versus post hoc justifications)18,19,20. Consequently, the risk of LLMs providing assistance to illegal activities remains substantially underestimated, and how LLMs perform across diverse illicit contexts is still largely unexplored. To better characterize the risk of LLMs assisting illegal activities, we draw on the legal concept of complicity, which involves participation in an illegal act through aiding, abetting, or facilitating its commission20, and introduce the notion of *complicit facilitation* to describe the specific behavior of LLMs providing assistance to users’ illicit instructions through their responses. To systematically study this phenomenon, we develop an automated pipeline that constructs realistic and diverse illicit user instructions from real-world court judgments and established legal frameworks (Fig. 1), differing from previous research that relies on manually-designed prompts or model-generated prompts expanded from limited sets of keywords10,13. LLMs.content: A newly published computational research initiative has introduced an open-access dataset containing 1,260 simulated urban experience narratives to systematically investigate how contemporary large language models represent human social interactions and daily routines across 21 major metropolitan centers worldwide. Developed by an international research team, the project addresses the methodological challenge of evaluating artificial intelligence as an analytical lens for global urban environments across distinct socioeconomic and cultural contexts. Rather than attempting to replicate living urban systems or dynamic multi-agent societies, the researchers established a standardized, static cross-sectional corpus that benchmarks how different foundation models encode geographic nuance, spatial dynamics, and interpersonal encounters. The resulting corpus spans seven global regions and captures weekend routines through four distinct sociodemographic actor profiles. By comparing narrative coherence, cross-model variability, and representational fidelity under rigorous experimental controls, the benchmark establishes a foundational framework for probing the epistemic capabilities and computational constraints of generative models within computational social science. Accelerating urbanization throughout the twentieth century fundamentally restructured global population distribution, establishing cities as the predominant human habitat and making the relationship between built environments and social behavior a primary scientific focus. Urban systems present exceptional structural complexity, historically forcing scholars to balance qualitative observational methods that offer contextual richness against large-scale quantitative frameworks designed for macro-level pattern detection. While traditional empirical techniques provide crucial localized depth, they remain sharply constrained by limited scale, high operational costs, and poor cross-city comparability. Conversely, conventional data-driven urban metrics achieve broad scalability but routinely omit sociocultural texture and subtle behavioral dynamics. Emerging developments in generative artificial intelligence present an alternative paradigm by enabling neural models to synthesize descriptive prose encoding spatial, structural, and cultural assumptions. The newly introduced dataset leverages these generative capabilities not to replace empirical observation, but to establish a controlled computational testbed capable of isolating how machine learning architectures interpret spatial structures. To construct a globally distributed and statistically balanced corpus, the investigators deployed a fully crossed factorial experimental design encompassing 21 global cities situated across seven designated geographic regions. These continental zones comprise the Asia-Pacific region, East Asia-China, Europe, Latin America, the Middle East and North Africa, North America, and Sub-Saharan Africa. Within each geographic territory, three prominent metropolitan centers were identified using model-guided random prompting, yielding an urban sample dominated by internationally recognized metropolitan hubs. Narrative generation was systematically distributed across three distinct open-weight neural architectures: Mistral Nemo 12B, Llama 3.3 70B, and Falcon Mamba 7B. For every unique combination of urban center and actor archetype, each model executed five independent generative simulations. AI Product.title: AI vendors say companies are measuring ROI the wrong way. What will convince CFOs to keep paying? - Fast Company
AI Product.titleZh: AI vendors say companies are measuring ROI the wrong way. What will convince CFOs to keep paying? - Fast Company
AI Product.content: Artificial intelligence companies want their customers to use more AI. Their customers want AI to help them spend less money. That creates a tricky dynamic for an industry whose revenue depends on selling more of a technology that’s supposed to make businesses more efficient. As CFOs prepare their 2027 budgets, the question is becoming harder to avoid: Is all this AI spending actually paying off? The industry’s preferred measures of progress offer an incomplete answer. Salesforce reports that its technology has performed 7 billion agentic work units, which count activities such as invoking a tool or completing a reasoning chain. A single business outcome can require many such units. Meanwhile, ServiceNow told investors on October 28 that its internal AI use generates more than $1 billion in annualized value, double its estimate at the end of 2025. Those figures help vendors make their case to investors but offer buyers less certainty about what they’re paying for. More automated activity can mean useful work—or repeated attempts to complete the same task. At Infosys, that tension is already affecting revenue expectations. AI revenue rose 29% from the previous quarter and reached 10.5% of sales, yet the company cut its full-year growth outlook to 1%-2% amid pricing pressure and demands for greater productivity. When AI lets a client buy the same service for less, the savings strengthen the client’s case for investing in AI while reducing the supplier’s contract value. New AI business must make up for the revenue lost as existing work becomes cheaper. In a survey of 260 finance executives, the cloud cost management company CloudZero found that two-thirds said their boards required proof of returns before approving further AI investment. Yet a separate survey from Protiviti, a management consultancy, found that only 35% of finance organizations considered themselves effective at measuring AI returns. In conversations with *Fast Company*, enterprise AI leaders described how competing definitions of success are shaping pricing and contract renewals. Outcome-based pricing offers little protection when a vendor counts a problem as resolved but leaves the customer with more work. Higher consumption bills are difficult to justify when a cheaper model delivers the same result. To secure another year of spending, suppliers may need to show customers which expenses they can eliminate, even when that means reducing their own fees. ## Snowflake tells some customers to spend less on AI Snowflake’s CEO, Sridhar Ramaswamy, argues that rising AI consumption is worthwhile only when it leads to operational improvements and replaces existing costs. Snowflake reported $1.49 billion in product revenue for its second fiscal quarter of 2027, up 37% from a year earlier, and 126% net revenue retention.

Infra & Chips.content: # Nvidia’s $228 Billion Data Center Bet: Three Things to Know ### Key Takeaways - Chipmaker has disclosed up to $118 billion in guarantees - Leases and equity investments add a further $110 billion By BloombergNEF (BloombergNEF) — Jensen Huang has left Nvidia with a data center financing ecosystem worth over $228billion, including more than twice the credit support of any other major data center backer. With Huang’s ouster, the future of this financing strategy – what the industry calls “balance-sheet-as-a-service”– will hinge on his replacement’s direction. A pivot by the chip giant could slow financing for neoclouds and other data center firms highly reliant on its support. During its 3Q earnings call Tuesday, Nvidia said existing customer commitments and operations wouldcontinue without interruption, but did not respond to BloombergNEF’s earlier request for comment on future financial support. Interim Chief Executive Officer Colette Kress noted during the call that Nvidia would betaking a “very strong look” at the types of fi rms it supports going forward, saying that “a lot of things have changed” over the last quarter. The chipmaker has used multiple financing mechanisms such as lease agreements, guarantees and equity investments to back neoclouds and AI labs. A pullback from these approaches would leave some data center developers with higher financing costs, fewer viable projects or a greater need for support from hyperscalers and private capital. Companies developing data centers have raised at least $1.8 trillion between 2020 and 1H2026, according to recent BNEF analysis. ### Nvidia dominates credit support Nvidia has committed up to $118 billion to backstop its customers, a key condition for less credit worthy data center developers to unlock financing. The total is far larger than other players following the same strategy, such as Meta and Google, according to BNEF data. Chief among Nvidia’s deals is a $105 billion residual value guarantee for the initial 4.25 gigawatts of OpenAI’s planned campus with SB Energy in Ohio. The guarantee covers any shortfall between a minimum lease value and proceeds from a replacement lease or sale if OpenAI becomes insolvent or stops paying. SB Energy, a subsidiary of SoftBank, agreed to enter the lease, power-purchase and transmission agreements only if Nvidia provided the backstop. While valuable, Nvidia’s guarantees have limits. In the company’s latest earnings call, Kress clarified that its OpenAI guarantee is for the operational data center, not construction or development, and would cease to apply in the event of delays. ### Nvidia’s backing extends beyond guarantees Nvidia established a $500 billion financing platform for AI infrastructure with BlackRock, Goldman Sachs, Blackstone, KKR, Apollo and Brookfield, agreeing to provide support of up to 25% for selected deals, creating a maximum exposure of $125 billion. That support, called a residual value guarantee, provides a recovery floor for lenders by covering the shortfall between outstanding debt and the liquidated asset value in the event of developer insolvency or default. Nvidia has committed to $20 billion of data center leases as a bridge for its customers, storing capacity on its balance sheet before transferring it later. One example is Hut 8’s Beacon Point campus in Texas. Nvidia is the lease holder, while neo cloud Lambda will use the facility to serve an approximately $35 billion Anthropic cloud contract, according to The Wall Street Journal. Hut 8 utilized Nvidia’s off take agreement to raise $4.25 billion. Nvidia also serves as a flexible off taker for several of its neocloud customers, signing up to $32 billion in AI compute commitments. These favorable agreements give neoclouds a revenue floor on part of their capacity, helping them raise debt, while allowing them to resell that capacity to higher-paying third parties. Nvidia earns revenue on the upfront hardware sale and may receive a share of neocloud revenue ...

Infra & Chips.content: This week, Nvidia dispelled fears of the AI trade slowing with one simple number; fiscal 2028 revenue growth is guided to be 75% up from 70% despite a higher FY27 revenue base. Vera Rubin generated $20 billion in revenue in its first quarter of production shipments, which is Nvidia’s fastest ramp ever. The Q4 guide is softer than it appears as it includes an extra week. If we adjust to a 13-week quarter, it works out to $121 billion or roughly 4% sequential growth after three quarters of 20% sequential growth. The guide excludes $2.4 billion in licensed Hopper sales to China that contributed to Q3. Don’t sweat it, though; we’ve been here before. When Nvidia transitions between product generations, the market typically panics as it reads the lull as a permanent slowdown. In fact, some of my very best AI entries have occurred during the pause between generations. As of now, Rubin’s first quarter is nearly double Blackwell’s at $20 billion compared to $11 billion, respectively. Management also stated the ramp is “off to an extraordinary start. During the Blackwell transition, sequential growth slowed to 12% in each of the first two quarters of the ramp, then to 6% in Q2 when H20 sales from China went to zero. After that, sales re-accelerated to 22% and 19% QoQ. Margins are the weaker part of the story, but you’d have to be living under a rock not to expect memory costs to weigh on profitability. Gross margin is expected to fall from 74.9% to 71%-72% in Q4, which the CFO said was a bottom with margins expected to return to 72%-73%. Now that we’ve gotten some of the obligatory earnings coverage out of the way, let’s talk about what’s really on everyone’s minds – is the AI trade over? Or perhaps equally concerning, is AI slowing to the point the glory years are behind us? Before we discuss the facts, I would encourage investors to pay close attention to who is spreading fear, uncertainty and doubt when the underlying fundamentals remain strong. Valid concerns are worth considering, but investors should deeply question why the concerns are brought up after a steep selloff rather than before it. Psychology is a major component of successful investing, and there is not a more important time to protect your mindset than when stock prices are at a multi-year low. Case in point, you’d have to go back at least 10 years to find Nvidia trading this low; therefore, it’s reasonable that many years go by until investors see some of these valuations again. Infra & Chips.content: # **Bridging Facility and Compute Operations in AI Data Centers: A Public-Evidence Comparison of DCIM Software Vendors and an Integrated Operations Platform** **Abstract** AI data centers combine dense GPU clusters, liquid cooling and megawatt-scale electrical plant, yet the software used to operate them remains split between data center infrastructure management (DCIM) tools that see the facility and cluster managers that see the GPUs. This paper compares nine commercial offerings — Schneider Electric EcoStruxure IT, Vertiv Environet, Sunbird dcTrack and Power IQ, Eaton Brightlayer Data Centers, Nlyte (Carrier), Hyperview, Siemens Datacenter Clarity LC, ABB Ability Data Center Automation and NVIDIA Mission Control — with AIDC, an integrated platform developed by the author that spans facility, compute and commercial operations. Using only public vendor documentation collected on 13 November 2026, we code each product against a twelve-item capability framework organised in three layers and analyse pricing units, delivery models and price transparency. The eight DCIM vendors score between 2 and 7.5 of 12 and cover none of the compute or commercial capabilities; NVIDIA Mission Control covers GPU health and scheduling but only 1 of the 9 facility items. AIDC scores 9.5, the highest total, but its facility-layer score (6.5) trails Schneider and Hyperview (7), owing to missing SNMP collection, a partial asset register and no 3D or CFD views. Only ABB and AIDC allocate energy to tenants. Only one vendor publishes a price list, and four publish no prices. We argue that the facility–compute divide, rather than feature depth within either side, is the main gap in the current market, and we derive a prioritised list of capabilities an integrated platform must still add. Because the author develops AIDC, we report the coding rules, the evidence base and the threats to validity in full. **Keywords:** data center infrastructure management; AI data center; GPU cluster operations; energy management; power usage effectiveness; software licensing; vendor comparison ## 1. Introduction The facilities that train and serve large AI models differ from the enterprise data centers for which most operations software was designed. Racks of accelerators draw several times the power of conventional server racks, many require direct-to-chip liquid cooling through coolant distribution units (CDUs), and the economic output of the facility is measured in GPU-hours and tokens rather than in rack space leased. Operators of such facilities therefore need to see, in one place, the state of the electrical and mechanical plant, the health and allocation of the GPUs, and the usage that is ultimately billed to tenants \[1]. The software market has grown up along a different line. Data center infrastructure management (DCIM) products monitor power, cooling and environmental equipment, maintain asset records and plan capacity. GPU cluster managers schedule jobs, track accelerator health and, increasingly, manage power at the node level. Billing for AI services is usually handled by a third system again. The operator of an AI data center consequently assembles several products whose data models do not meet. This paper asks how far current commercial offerings close that gap. We pose three research questions: 1\. **RQ1.** Which operational capabilities do current DCIM and AI-cluster products cover, according to their public documentation? 2\. **RQ2.** How are these products packaged, delivered and priced, and how transparent is that pricing? 3\. **RQ3.** Where does an integrated platform that spans facility, compute and commercial operations stand relative to these products, and which capabilities should it add first? We answer these questions with a structured comparison of nine commercial products and AIDC, an integrated platform developed by the author. Section 2 reviews the product categories involved. Section 3 describes the evidence base and the coding framework. ...

Racks of accelerators draw several times the power of conventional server racks, many require direct-to-chip liquid cooling through coolant distribution units (CDUs), and the economic output of the facility is measured in GPU-hours and tokens rather than in rack space leased. Operators of such facilities therefore need to see, in one place, the state of the electrical and mechanical plant, the health and allocation of the GPUs, and the usage that is ultimately billed to tenants \[1]. The software market has grown up along a different line. Data center infrastructure management (DCIM) products monitor power, cooling and environmental equipment, maintain asset records and plan capacity. GPU cluster managers schedule jobs, track accelerator health and, increasingly, manage power at the node level. Billing for AI services is usually handled by a third system again. The operator of an AI data center consequently assembles several products whose data models do not meet. This paper asks how far current commercial offerings close that gap. We pose three research questions: 1\. **RQ1.** Which operational capabilities do current DCIM and AI-cluster products cover, according to their public documentation? 2\. **RQ2.** How are these products packaged, delivered and priced, and how transparent is that pricing? 3\. **RQ3.** Where does an integrated platform that spans facility, compute and commercial operations stand relative to these products, and which capabilities should it add first? We answer these questions with a structured comparison of nine commercial products and AIDC, an integrated platform developed by the author. Section 2 reviews the product categories involved.
